name: Dinka, Northern/Padang variety within a pan-Dinka analysis
confidence_why: Malou 1988, Tucker & Bryan 1966 and Blum 2023 all describe Dinka, including the Padang and Ngok varieties, as a tone language with three or four contrastive tones, and the only disagreement concerns Malou's side remark that each word also carries one non-contrastive stress of unstudied placement, which acoustic work on other dialects reported by Remijsen & Manyang 2009 and by van Urk & Chong 2025 doubts.
catalog_citation: Malou, Job. 1988. Dinka Vowel System. Publications in Linguistics 82. Dallas: Summer Institute of Linguistics and the University of Texas at Arlington. (ERIC microfiche scan, open item archive.org/details/micro_IA41152914_0785)
catalog_locator: Sec. 2.2 'The Phonological Word', pp. 9-10; sec. 2 intro exclusion p. 8; sec. 2.3 tone statement p. 10; scope statement (four varieties incl. 'Northern, known as Padan, which is Donjol based') p. 1.
catalog_quote: Matters of juncture, stress, and intonation, which could be discussed under syntagmatic phonology and emphatic features, are not of concern in this discussion. ... [2.2 The Phonological Word] Described in terms of the elements distributed in it and the features which characterize it, the phonological word is the unit of stress placement in the phonological hierarchy. Each phonological word has one and only one stress. The factors that condition stress have not been studied and, as mentioned, are not the concern of this discussion. It is clear, however, that stress is neither contrastive nor used at all in connection with semantic emphasis in Dinka. The final margin of the phonological word is characterized by potential pause. The phonological word is the level of distribution of the syllable: one syllable is stressed in each word. ... [2.3 The Syllable] ... the syllable in Dinka is the unit of tone placement. Every syllable carries one and only one tone.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: Dinka (all four major varieties, explicitly including Northern/Padang) has exactly one culminative stress per phonological word; the source does not say which syllable carries it ('the factors that condition stress have not been studied'), only that stress is non-contrastive and not used for emphasis. Lexical and morphological prosody is carried by tone, vowel length and voice quality (for the Ngok-Sobat variety of nort2815 see Blum 2023 ch.5: four tones L/H/HL/LH, three vowel lengths, two voice qualities). Later work on other Dinka varieties doubts a stress system altogether (Remijsen & Manyang 2009 fn.5: no acoustic support in Luanyjang; van Urk & Chong 2025: 'Dinka lacks an obvious stress system'); a 2025 instrumental investigation of Dinka stress (Blum et al. dataset) has no published result yet.
new_statements.exceptions: None; the author states that the conditioning factors have not been studied and that stress, juncture and intonation are outside the scope of the book.
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the phonological word (bounded by potential pause); the examples in (5), pp. 9-10, are two-word citation phrases each carrying a single stress mark (e.g. 'mony dit 'old man', ' yok lac 'pregnant cows'), so the statement concerns word-level prominence in citation forms, not phrase-level or sentence intonation (treated separately under 2.1 with downdrift).
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted statement is pan-Dinka, not specific to Northeastern Dinka: Malou (1988: 1) says his analysis covers the four major varieties 'Eastern, which is Bor based; Northern, known as Padan, which is Donjol based; Southern which is Agar based; and Western which is Rek based', so the Northern/Padang variety (Dongjol, dong1295, a dialect of nort2815) is explicitly within scope, but the author's own variety is not stated (the compilers Dinka's internal-evidence check suggests it is neither Rek nor Agar). The same Malou passage has been recorded for sout2832 (Southwestern) and sout2834 (Southeastern); the catalog should treat it as one source claim covering all Dinka lects rather than four independent descriptions. The only first-hand descriptions of nort2815 dialects proper are tone/length studies that do not mention stress: Blum 2023 ch.5 (Ngok of the Padang cluster, speakers from the Malakal area = Ngok-Sobat ngok1245; held by the project) and Remijsen 2014 (Ageer agee1238; abstract only).

new_statements.rule_in_words: For the Nilotic languages treated jointly in the chapter (DINKA, NUER, N. LWO = Shilluk, S. LWO), stress falls on the word stem and never on a prefix or suffix; tone is separately lexical and grammatical (sec. 2a: three tone levels High, Mid, Low; 'In DINKA-NUER and SHILLUK at least there are three specific tonemes'). No Dinka-specific or Padang-specific stress rule is given.
new_statements.exceptions: None for Dinka; a possible relationship between stress and vowel length is noted for Southern Lwo only (cross-reference § 14 (i)).
new_statements.identity_note: Tucker & Bryan 1966 treat DINKA, NUER, Northern Lwo (Shilluk) and Southern Lwo jointly; Dinka examples are from the Bor dialect (Southeastern Dinka) unless otherwise stated, and Padang (the nort2815 cluster) appears only as a manuscript source (Trudinger) and in a few comparative forms; Ngok is not named. Malou 1988 (catalog source) is pan-Dinka and explicitly includes 'Northern, known as Padan[g], which is Donjol based' (= Dongjol, under nort2815). Blum 2023 ch. 5 describes Ngok (Padang cluster) tone only, with no stress statement.

new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the catalog classification tonal (Malou 1988): confirms Dinka is a tone language and adds a stress statement. Compatible with Tucker & Bryan 1966 sec. 2b ('stress is on the Stem.. never on its Prefixes or Suffixes'): Gilley's stress mark falls on the verb root after the a- prefix. Tension with Malou 1988 ('stress is neither contrastive nor used.. with semantic emphasis'): Gilley uses 'stress' for a CONTRASTIVE root-level feature (2sg vs 3sg readers; sg/pl), but she states explicitly that the term labels Andersen's vowel-length grades, so this is a different notion of 'stress' (length-grade label vs Malou's one culminative stress per phonological word), not a different placem…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Dinka is tonal (two level tones plus HL, L-fall and rising contours; tone marks clause structure, valency and some sg/pl pairs). Gilley's 'stress' is a property of the monosyllabic CVC root/word, realized as shortening of the vowel to about half: it is her two-way relabelling of Andersen's (1993) three degrees of vowel length (extra-short vs short, short vs long) and it carries grammatical contrasts (2sg vs 3sg readers on verbs, exx. 1-2/47-48; sg vs pl on nouns, exx. 41-42). Where a verb carries the present-tense prefix a-, the stress mark is written before the root syllable (á'mòc), i.e. stress sits on the root, not the prefix. No positional word-stress rule for polysyllables is stated; the orthography proposal marks the UNstressed word with a word-final apostrophe (amoc').
new_statements.exceptions: Roots with an underlyingly short vowel cannot lengthen: singular is 'extra short', plural 'just short' or 'lowered' (diphthongized, Duerksen 1989), ex. 43 rïc / rïc~riëc; Dinka speakers reject a three-way length analysis and hear a two-way distinction.
new_statements.identity_note: Gilley 2004: Dinka examples are Rek (South-Western Dinka), stated to be representative of Rek, Bor, Agaar and Padang; SIL entry 7859 lists dip (Northeastern Dinka = Padang) among subject languages; the paper also treats Shilluk. Tucker & Bryan 1966: Dinka examples from the Bor dialect unless stated, Padang only via Trudinger's MS grammar and scattered forms; the stress sentence is made for Dinka, Nuer, N. Lwo and S. Lwo jointly. Neither is a dedicated description of Northern/Padang Dinka.

tone_statements.quote: The Ngok dialect of Dinka has four underlying tonal categories, like the example above in Table 2. The tones are the level categories Low (L, v̀) and High (H, v́), and the contour tone categories Fall (HL, v̂) and Rise (LH, v̌). … the contour tones are each analyzed, across dialects of Dinka, as consisting of one Low tone element and one High element … the dialect has four underlying tone categories, but only three surface categories. readall_conflicts: No two opened sources give different placements: Malou 1988 (catalog) gives no placement and says stress is non-contrastive with unstudied conditioning; Tucker & Bryan 1966 (snippets, group-level for Nilotic) put stress on the stem and never on affixes, which is compatible and, for a 'largely monosyllabic' language (Blum 2023, sec. 2.2.1), nearly vacuous. Gilley 2004 was not opened. A tension exists with later instrumental work already held by the project in the sibling Dinka directories but not among this item's listed works: Remijsen & Manyang 2009 (fn. 5: Gilley's 2003 'stress' is the morphological short grade, and Remijsen & Gilley 2008 found no acoustic support in Luanyjang) and van Urk & Chong 2025 ('Dinka lacks an obvious stress system'), which cast doubt on whether Dinka has word stress at all; Blum et al. 2025 announce a stress dataset with no stated result. None of these concerns the Padang cluster specifically. No disagreement on placement. The only tension is terminological: Malou 1988 (catalog record) says each phonological word has exactly one stress and that stress is neither contrastive nor emphatic, while Gilley 2004 uses 'stress' for a contrastive feature of the CVC root (stressed = vowel shortened to about half; 2sg vs 3sg readers, some sg/pl nouns) and says outright that the term stands for Andersen's (1993) vowel-length grades, which Malou and Andersen treat as length, not stress. tone.says: Ngok Dinka: four underlying tones Low, High, Fall, Rise on the syllable; three surface categories (High and Rise neutralize utterance-finally after Low); contours = L+H elements; H becomes L after H.

sources.note: Comparative-historical tonology across six Dinka dialects (Luanyjang, Agar, Bor South, Ngok, Twic, Aliap; Ngok, Bor South and Twic are the author's own data; 'There are also two Ngok dialects; the one discussed here is part of the Padang cluster', AAM p.4).
